newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Atmosphere ugly as rival Serbian demos clash.
newsitem.headline: Atmosphere ugly as rival Serbian demos clash.

text.p: Street fighting between government and opposition demonstrators swept central Belgrade on Tuesday after Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic brought thousands of supporters to the capital in a show of strength.

Eyewitnesses said rival groups battered each other with sticks and iron bars as brushfire scuffles erupted among the crowds converging on the headquarters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition.
Police did not intervene as 35 days of peaceful Zajedno protests against election fraud by Milosevic's ruling socialists turned ugly.
The Socialist Party (SPS) called its demonstration at the same place where Zajedno has held daily demonstrations in what opposition sources said was a clear act of provocation.
There were fears that the SPS might use the violence as an excuse to ban future demonstrations or even to declare a state of emergency.
Milosevic, under threat of Western reprisals, has not so far used his police against the demonstrations, the biggest since 1992 when he used tanks to quell unrest.
The authorities ferried demonstraters by bus from across the country in an effort to reassert Milosevic's authority with a massive show of support.

Some 40,000 students who have been holding parallel demonstrations against Milosevic gathered about 1,000 metres (yards) from the Zajedno offices but said they would avoid all contact with the socialist rally.

Zajedno, backed by the United States and other Western countries, is trying to force Milosevic to admit its victories in Belgrade and 14 other towns at local elections on November 17, breaking half a century of socialist rule.
Its peaceful daily demonstrations, which reached a peak of 250,000 people, have grown into the worst crisis the authoritarian Milosevic has faced in nine years of power.
Vuksanovic told Reuters: "(Milosevic) is out of his mind. He has brought thousands of people to Belgrade, people who are not informed about this situation.
"In some parts of Belgrade, they have already started fights. I am afraid it could be the beginning of civil war in Serbia and all responsibility is on Milosevic's side."

Vuksanovic said an SPS crowd shouting outside Zajedno's headquarters three hours before the demonstration was due to begin were from Pec, a hardline nationalist redoubt in the southern republic of Kosovo.
Kosovo Serbs were the shock troops who brought Milosevic to power on a tide of nationalism that set off the disintegration of former Yugoslavia in 1991-92.
Up to 10,000 other pro-Milosevic demonstrators were milling in the nearby Republic Square in case Zajedno switched its protest there.
As the atmosphere of intimdation grew, the SPO party -- a Zajedno partner -- said its Belgrade bookshop was attacked by a group of unidentified men, at least three of them armed.
Zajedno earlier rejected an appeal by Serbian Orthodox Patriarch Pavle to suspend its demonstration after he warned that the conflict risked turning into an armed confrontation.
In a swipe at Milosevic, he coupled his plea with praise for the opposition's restraint during the campaign of protests.

Zajedno was told the SPS mobilised 10,000 buses to bring demonstrators including factory workers for "a spontaneous assembly of supporters of the peaceful and consistent policy of President Milosevic".
The buses travelled under police escort.

Although the opposition rallies in Belgrade and other towns have been peaceful, the BETA news agency reported scuffles on Monday in Valjevo, near Belgrade, when 20,000 Zajedno activists took to the streets in response to a socialist rally.

Workers have mostly ignored the intelligentsia-led marches. Opposition sources said factory hands were threatened with reprisals, including the withdrawal of lay-off pay, if they refused to attend the socialist rally.
